title: Adam and Christ: two heads of humanity

type.name: Adam
type.summary: The first human, formed from the dust and given life by God's breath. He was placed in the garden to keep it and to obey one command. His disobedience brought death, toil and exile, and his children inherited his likeness.

antitype.name: Christ, the last Adam
antitype.summary: Jesus is the head of a new humanity. Where Adam's one act of disobedience brought condemnation and death to many, Jesus' one act of obedience brings righteousness and life. Adam became a living being; Christ became a life-giving Spirit.

correspondences.type: One man's act affects all who belong to him
correspondences.antitype: One man's obedience affects all who belong to him

correspondences.type: Tested in a garden and fails
correspondences.antitype: Tested in a wilderness and in the garden of Gethsemane and holds firm

correspondences.type: Brings death into the world
correspondences.antitype: Brings resurrection life

correspondences.type: Made from earth, bears an earthly image
correspondences.antitype: From heaven; believers will bear his heavenly image

correspondences.type: Given dominion over creation
correspondences.antitype: Given all authority, with everything put under his feet

differences: Paul stresses that the two are not equal: 'the free gift is not like the trespass' (Rom 5:15). Adam's act was one sin leading to condemnation; Christ's gift answers many sins and brings justification. Adam was a created man; Christ is the Lord from heaven.

fathers.note: Developed recapitulation: Christ goes back over the whole human story Adam spoiled and gets it right at every point, summing humanity up in himself.

Read Romans 5 as the root of the doctrine of original sin: all humanity was somehow 'in Adam'. This reading shaped the Western church but is debated by Eastern Orthodox theologians, who speak of inherited mortality rather than inherited guilt.

plain: Paul says Adam was a 'pattern' (Greek *typos*) of the one to come. Think of two family trees. Everyone starts in Adam's family, which ends in death. Jesus starts a new family, and those joined to him share his life. This is the clearest example of a type in the whole Bible, because Paul uses the very word.
caution: How exactly humanity is 'in Adam' (guilt, corruption, mortality, or all three) is debated between Western and Eastern traditions, and modern discussion of human origins adds further questions. The typology itself does not settle those debates.

title: Eve and the bride: the church from Christ's side

type.name: Eve, the bride of Adam
type.summary: God takes a rib from the sleeping Adam and builds the woman. Adam greets her as bone of his bones, and the two become one flesh. She is named the mother of all living.

antitype.name: The church, bride of Christ
antitype.summary: Christ loves the church, gives himself for her and makes her holy, as a husband with his bride. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says it is a great mystery about Christ and the church.

correspondences.type: Adam falls into a deep sleep
correspondences.antitype: Christ sleeps in death on the cross

correspondences.type: The bride is taken from Adam's opened side
correspondences.antitype: Blood and water flow from Christ's pierced side, read as the sacraments that build the church

correspondences.type: Two become one flesh
correspondences.antitype: The church is Christ's body, united with him

correspondences.type: Eve is deceived by the serpent
correspondences.antitype: Paul fears the church may be led astray as Eve was

differences: Eve was deceived and shared in the fall; the bride of Revelation is pictured finally pure and ready. Paul never calls Eve a typos; he draws the marriage analogy from Genesis 2:24 rather than from Eve as a person. The 'side' link (John 19:34) is a later reading, not stated in the NT.

fathers.note: Compared Adam's sleep and opened side to Christ's death and pierced side, from which the church, the true mother of the living, was formed.
Repeatedly said the church was formed from the side of the sleeping Christ just as Eve was formed from the side of sleeping Adam.

source.author: Augustine
source.title: Tractates on the Gospel of John

fathers.note: Paired Eve not only with the church but with Mary: Eve's disobedience was untied by Mary's obedience. This Eve–Mary parallel is a separate, traditional typology.

plain: The Bible begins and ends with a wedding. In Genesis a bride is made from the first man's side; in Revelation the church is presented as the bride of the Lamb. Paul says the marriage of Genesis 2 points to Christ and the church.
caution: The NT links marriage in Genesis to Christ and the church, but the details (the sleep, the side, the rib) are developed by the Fathers. The Eve–Mary parallel is traditional and especially important in Catholic and Orthodox devotion; Protestants generally do not adopt it.

title: Abel's blood and the blood that speaks better

type.name: Abel, the murdered righteous brother
type.summary: Abel offers an acceptable sacrifice and is killed by his jealous brother Cain. God says Abel's blood cries out from the ground.

antitype.name: Jesus, the righteous one killed by his brothers
antitype.summary: Jesus, the innocent one, is killed through the envy of his own people. His sprinkled blood speaks a better word than Abel's: not a cry for vengeance but a word of forgiveness and covenant.

correspondences.type: A shepherd who brings an acceptable offering
correspondences.antitype: The good shepherd who is himself the offering

correspondences.type: Killed by a brother out of envy
correspondences.antitype: Handed over out of envy (Mark 15:10)

correspondences.type: His blood cries from the ground
correspondences.antitype: His blood speaks from heaven

correspondences.type: First of the righteous martyrs
correspondences.antitype: Jesus names Abel's blood at the head of the line his generation will answer for

differences: Hebrews uses Abel by contrast: his blood calls for justice, Christ's blood brings mercy. Abel was a sinner like everyone else and his death achieved nothing for others; Christ's death is described as redemptive.

fathers.note: In his Easter sermon lists Abel among the figures in whom Christ suffered beforehand: murdered in Abel, bound in Isaac, sold in Joseph, exposed in Moses, hunted in David.
Read Cain and Abel as the start of the two cities: Cain founds an earthly city, Abel is a pilgrim, a figure of Christ and his people.

plain: Abel was the first person in the Bible to die, killed by his own brother. His blood 'cried out' for justice. Hebrews says Jesus' blood also speaks, but it says something better: it brings people near to God instead of calling down judgement.
caution: The NT text uses Abel more as a contrast than as a foreshadowing pattern. Calling Abel a 'type' is fair in the Fathers' sense, but the Hebrews link is comparative rather than a stated typos.

title: Enoch, the man who walked with God and was taken

type.name: Enoch
type.summary: Enoch walked with God and then 'was not, for God took him'. Hebrews says he was taken so that he should not see death, and Jude cites him as a prophet of judgement.

antitype.name: Christ's ascension and the hope of believers
antitype.summary: Later readers saw in Enoch a picture of a righteous person received into God's presence, foreshadowing Christ's ascension and the final transformation of believers who are alive at his return.

correspondences.type: Walks closely with God
correspondences.antitype: The Son lives in perfect communion with the Father

correspondences.type: Taken up without dying
correspondences.antitype: Those alive at Christ's coming are changed without dying

correspondences.type: Seventh from Adam, a preacher of coming judgement
correspondences.antitype: Christ announces and carries out the final judgement

differences: Enoch did not die; Christ did die and then rose before ascending, so the ascension is not a copy of Enoch's translation. The NT never calls Enoch a type of Christ; Hebrews uses him as an example of faith.

fathers.note: Cited Enoch (with Elijah) as evidence that God can preserve a human body in life, supporting bodily resurrection.
Several early writers identified Enoch and Elijah as the two witnesses of Revelation 11, who would return to die. This is tradition, not stated in Scripture.

plain: Enoch is famous for one line: he walked with God, and then God took him. Christians have seen him as a small preview of the hope that death does not have the last word, and that God can bring a person straight into his presence.
caution: This is a traditional, fairly light typology. The book of 1 Enoch, quoted in Jude, is canonical only in the Ethiopian Orthodox church; it should not be used to build NT typology. The Enoch-and-Elijah-as-two-witnesses idea is tradition.

title: Noah's ark and baptism

type.name: The ark through the flood
type.summary: God tells Noah to build an ark. Eight people and the animals are carried safely through the waters of judgement that destroy the old world, and they step out into a washed creation.

antitype.name: Baptism into Christ
antitype.summary: Peter says the water that saved Noah's family corresponds to baptism, which now saves, not by washing dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus.

correspondences.type: Waters of judgement on a corrupt world
correspondences.antitype: Baptism as dying to the old life

correspondences.type: Eight saved inside the ark
correspondences.antitype: Believers saved by being 'in Christ'

correspondences.type: A new world emerges from the water
correspondences.antitype: Rising to new life with the risen Christ

correspondences.type: The dove brings an olive leaf
correspondences.antitype: The Spirit descends like a dove at Jesus' baptism

differences: The flood killed the wicked; baptism is offered to them. Peter insists the saving power is not the water itself but Christ's resurrection and the pledge of a good conscience. The ark carried the righteous; the church holds sinners being made righteous.

fathers.note: Saw the eight people as pointing to the eighth day, the day of resurrection, and linked the wood of the ark to the wood of the cross.
Compared the dove returning to the ark with the Spirit coming to the baptised.
Read the ark as a figure of the church and even of Christ's body, with the door in its side matching the wound in Christ's side.

plain: Noah's family went through a world-ending flood and came out alive because they were inside the ark. Peter says baptism is like that: you pass through water that signals death to the old life, and you come out safe because you are joined to the risen Jesus.
caution: Peter's word is *antitypon*, so the link is explicit. What baptism actually does is debated (see /debates/baptism): sacramental traditions read 'baptism now saves you' strongly; others stress Peter's qualification that it is the appeal of a good conscience. The patristic idea that there is no salvation outside the ark-church is an application, not part of Peter's text.

title: Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem

type.name: Melchizedek
type.summary: A king of Salem and priest of God Most High who brings bread and wine to Abraham, blesses him, and receives a tenth of the spoils. Psalm 110 later speaks of a royal priest 'after the order of Melchizedek'.

antitype.name: Christ, the eternal high priest
antitype.summary: Hebrews argues that Jesus is a priest not from Levi's tribe but in Melchizedek's line: a king-priest whose priesthood rests on an indestructible life, so he lives forever to intercede.

correspondences.type: Both king and priest
correspondences.antitype: Christ is royal Son and high priest

correspondences.type: 'King of righteousness' and 'king of peace'
correspondences.antitype: Christ brings righteousness and peace

correspondences.type: No recorded genealogy, birth or death
correspondences.antitype: Christ's priesthood does not depend on ancestry and has no end

correspondences.type: Abraham, ancestor of Levi, pays him a tenth
correspondences.antitype: Christ's priesthood is greater than the Levitical one

correspondences.type: Brings out bread and wine
correspondences.antitype: Read by many traditions as foreshadowing the Lord's Supper

differences: Hebrews says Melchizedek was 'made like' the Son of God, not that he was the Son; the silence about his parents is an argument from what Genesis leaves out. Melchizedek blessed Abraham once; Christ offered himself once for all and intercedes forever.

fathers.note: Argued that the bread and wine Melchizedek offered prefigured the eucharist, and used it to insist the cup must contain wine.
Used Melchizedek's offering as evidence that the Christian sacraments are older than those of the Jews.

plain: Melchizedek appears for three verses in Genesis and disappears. Hebrews uses the mystery around him to make a point: Jesus is a priest of a different and higher kind than the priests descended from Aaron, because his priesthood rests on his endless life, not on family descent.
caution: Hebrews never mentions the bread and wine, so the eucharistic link is traditional. Some interpreters, ancient and modern, have argued Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ; most read Hebrews 7:3 as typology from the silence of Genesis. Qumran's 11QMelchizedek shows Jews of the time also speculated about him.

title: Isaac bound on Moriah

type.name: The binding of Isaac (the Akedah)
type.summary: God tests Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, his beloved and only son of promise. Isaac carries the wood up the mountain; Abraham says God will provide the lamb. At the last moment God stops him and provides a ram.

antitype.name: The Father giving his Son
antitype.summary: God did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us. Hebrews says Abraham reasoned God could raise the dead, and received Isaac back 'as a figure' of resurrection.

correspondences.type: A beloved, only son of promise
correspondences.antitype: God's beloved only Son

correspondences.type: Isaac carries the wood up the hill
correspondences.antitype: Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha

correspondences.type: 'God will provide the lamb'
correspondences.antitype: 'Behold the Lamb of God' (John 1:29)

correspondences.type: On the third day Abraham sees the place
correspondences.antitype: Raised on the third day

correspondences.type: Isaac received back as if from death
correspondences.antitype: Christ actually raised from death

differences: Isaac was not sacrificed; a substitute died instead. In the antitype there is no substitute for the Son: he is himself the substitute. Abraham's hand was stopped; the Father's was not.

fathers.note: Treated Isaac as a figure of Christ who was bound, and the ram as the one who was actually slain.
Preached that Isaac carrying the wood is like Christ carrying the cross, and that Isaac as priest and victim both pictures Christ.
Noted that Isaac carried the wood as Christ carried his cross.

plain: Abraham was asked to give up the son he loved most, and then God stopped him. Christians read the story as a rehearsal: what God did not require of Abraham, he did himself in giving Jesus. Paul's wording 'did not spare his own Son' seems to echo God's words to Abraham.
caution: Romans 8:32 echoes the Greek of Genesis 22:16 but does not name Isaac, and Hebrews 11:19 says 'figuratively' (*en parabolē*) about receiving Isaac back, not about the sacrifice as a whole. Jewish tradition developed the Akedah in its own way, sometimes stressing Isaac's willing consent. The identification of Moriah with the later temple mount rests on 2 Chr 3:1; with Golgotha it is tradition.

title: The ram caught in the thicket

type.name: The substitute ram
type.summary: Abraham looks up and sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He offers it in place of his son and names the place 'The LORD will provide'.

antitype.name: Christ the substitute
antitype.summary: Jesus dies in the place of others, the provision God makes so that the guilty go free.

correspondences.type: Dies in Isaac's place
correspondences.antitype: Dies in the place of sinners

correspondences.type: Caught in a thicket by its head
correspondences.antitype: Crowned with thorns

correspondences.type: Provided by God, not brought by Abraham
correspondences.antitype: God himself provides the sacrifice

differences: The ram was an animal with no will in the matter; Christ gave himself freely. Note that Abraham predicted a lamb and God provided a ram: the 'lamb' language waits for the NT.

fathers.note: Said the Lord was the lamb like the ram that Abraham saw caught in the bush, and that the bush pointed to the cross.
Connected the ram caught by its horns with Christ crowned with thorns.

plain: Isaac did not die because something died in his place. Christians see in the ram the simplest picture of what they believe about the cross: someone else took the death that was due.
caution: No NT text mentions the ram. The thorns-and-thicket link is a devotional observation from the Fathers, not an argument the NT makes. Whether 'substitution' is the main or only meaning of the cross is debated (see /debates/atonement).

title: Joseph: rejected brother, exalted saviour

type.name: Joseph son of Jacob
type.summary: Joseph is his father's beloved son, hated and sold by his brothers, falsely accused and imprisoned. He is then raised to the right hand of Pharaoh and saves many lives, including the brothers who betrayed him.

antitype.name: Jesus, rejected and exalted
antitype.summary: Jesus is rejected by his own, sold for silver, condemned though innocent, and then exalted to God's right hand, from where he offers forgiveness and life to those who rejected him.

correspondences.type: Beloved son of his father
correspondences.antitype: Beloved Son of the Father

correspondences.type: Sold by his brothers for twenty pieces of silver
correspondences.antitype: Sold by a disciple for thirty pieces of silver

correspondences.type: Falsely accused and counted among prisoners
correspondences.antitype: Falsely accused and crucified between criminals

correspondences.type: Raised to the right hand of the ruler
correspondences.antitype: Raised to the right hand of God

correspondences.type: 'You meant evil, God meant it for good, to save many lives'
correspondences.antitype: Human wickedness and God's plan meet in the cross

correspondences.type: Brothers do not recognise him at first
correspondences.antitype: His own did not receive him (John 1:11)

differences: Joseph had faults (his early boasting) and sometimes tested his brothers harshly. His saving work was about famine and food, not sin and death. He was not killed.

fathers.note: Lists Joseph as one in whom the Lord was sold beforehand.
Wrote a whole treatise on Joseph as a model of chastity and a figure of Christ.

plain: Joseph's story has the shape of the gospel: the favoured son is rejected by his brothers, goes down into the pit and prison, is raised to power, and uses it to save the very people who wronged him. The NT never says 'Joseph was a type', but Stephen tells his story as part of a pattern of Israel rejecting the deliverers God sent.
caution: This is one of the most popular types but has no explicit NT warrant. Stephen's speech (Acts 7) makes the 'rejected deliverer' pattern visible with Joseph and Moses, but it does not draw the line to Jesus in so many words. Popular preaching sometimes stretches it to every detail (the coat, the cup, Asenath as the gentile church).

title: Moses and the prophet like Moses

type.name: Moses
type.summary: Moses is saved as a baby from a king's massacre, called to lead Israel out of slavery, speaks with God face to face, gives the law and mediates the covenant. He promised that God would raise up a prophet like him.

antitype.name: Jesus, the prophet like Moses
antitype.summary: Peter and Stephen identify Jesus as the promised prophet like Moses. Hebrews says Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house; Christ is faithful as the Son over it.

correspondences.type: Escapes as an infant when Pharaoh kills Hebrew boys
correspondences.antitype: Escapes as an infant when Herod kills Bethlehem's boys

correspondences.type: Gives the law from a mountain
correspondences.antitype: Teaches with authority on a mountain (Matt 5-7)

correspondences.type: Mediator of the old covenant
correspondences.antitype: Mediator of a new covenant (Heb 9:15)

correspondences.type: Feeds the people with manna in the wilderness
correspondences.antitype: Feeds crowds in deserted places

correspondences.type: Face shines after meeting God
correspondences.antitype: Transfigured, with Moses present (Matt 17:1-3)

correspondences.type: Rejected by his own people at first
correspondences.antitype: Rejected by his own

differences: Moses was a sinner who was barred from the land; Jesus is presented as sinless. Moses brought a law that, as John says, came through him, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Moses was a servant in the house; Jesus is the Son over it.

fathers.note: Includes Moses exposed on the river among the figures of Christ's sufferings.
Wrote the *Life of Moses*, reading his whole career as a picture of the soul's ascent to God, with many Christ-figures along the way.

plain: Moses promised that one day God would send another prophet like him, and the Jews of Jesus' day were still waiting for that figure. The apostles say Jesus is that prophet. Matthew especially tells Jesus' early life so that it echoes Moses' story.
caution: In its original setting Deuteronomy 18 can be read as a promise of a continuing line of prophets; the NT reads it as fulfilled supremely in one prophet. Matthew's Moses-parallels are widely recognised but not all are stated; some (five discourses matching five books) are scholarly proposals.

title: Aaron and the great high priest

type.name: Aaron the high priest
type.summary: Aaron is anointed as Israel's first high priest. He wears the names of the tribes on his shoulders and breastplate, offers sacrifices, and once a year enters the Most Holy Place with blood to make atonement.

antitype.name: Jesus our high priest
antitype.summary: Jesus is the high priest who sympathises with our weakness yet is without sin. He offered himself once for all, entered heaven itself, and always lives to intercede.

correspondences.type: Called by God, not self-appointed
correspondences.antitype: Christ did not exalt himself but was appointed

correspondences.type: Carries the tribes' names before God
correspondences.antitype: Represents his people before the Father

correspondences.type: Enters the Most Holy Place once a year
correspondences.antitype: Enters heaven once for all

correspondences.type: Offers the blood of animals
correspondences.antitype: Offers his own blood

correspondences.type: Must offer first for his own sins
correspondences.antitype: Has no sins of his own to offer for

differences: Hebrews is mostly about contrast: Aaron's priests died and were replaced, needed to sacrifice for themselves, served in a copy of the heavenly sanctuary, and repeated sacrifices that could not cleanse the conscience. Christ is said to be different on every count. Hebrews also places Jesus in Melchizedek's order, not Aaron's.

fathers.note: Preached on Leviticus 16, reading the high priest entering the sanctuary as Christ entering heaven with his own blood.
Used the ordered Levitical priesthood as a model for order in the church's ministry.

plain: Israel's high priest stood between God and the people. Hebrews says Jesus does that job perfectly and permanently. Where Aaron went into a tent once a year with animal blood, Jesus went into God's presence once for all with his own.
caution: Whether Christian ministers are 'priests' in a sense continuous with Aaron is debated between Catholic/Orthodox and Protestant traditions. Hebrews itself speaks of Christ's unique priesthood and of all believers offering sacrifices of praise (Heb 13:15).

title: The Passover lamb

type.name: The Passover lamb
type.summary: On the night of the exodus each household kills an unblemished lamb, marks the doorposts with its blood, and eats it. The destroyer passes over the marked houses. Not a bone of the lamb is to be broken.

antitype.name: Christ our Passover
antitype.summary: Paul says Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. John has Jesus die as the Passover lambs are prepared and notes that none of his bones were broken. The Last Supper is set at Passover.

correspondences.type: Lamb without blemish
correspondences.antitype: A lamb without blemish or spot (1 Pet 1:19)

correspondences.type: Blood on the door shields from death
correspondences.antitype: Christ's blood rescues from judgement

correspondences.type: No bone broken
correspondences.antitype: Soldiers do not break Jesus' legs

correspondences.type: Eaten in a meal that remembers deliverance
correspondences.antitype: The Lord's Supper remembers Christ's death

correspondences.type: Old leaven cleared out of the house
correspondences.antitype: Believers clear out malice and wickedness

differences: The Passover lamb was not originally a sin offering; it was a protective sign and a meal. The NT fuses Passover with other sacrifice ideas. Israel repeated Passover every year; Christ died once.

fathers.note: His Easter homily is a full reading of Exodus 12 as the type and Christ as the reality. He compares the type to an artist's model that is set aside once the real statue is finished.
Noted the lamb was roasted on crossed spits, which he took as a figure of the cross.

plain: On the night Israel left Egypt, the blood of a lamb on the door meant death passed over that house. The first Christians, many of them Jews, saw Jesus' death at Passover and said: he is our lamb. This is why Easter in many languages is still called by the Passover name (Pascha).
caution: Whether the Last Supper was itself a Passover meal (the Synoptics) or held the day before (John's timing) is a long-running historical question. Melito's sermon also contains harsh language against the Jewish people that later fed anti-Judaism and should be read critically.

title: Crossing the Red Sea and baptism

type.name: The crossing of the sea
type.summary: Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, Israel walks through on dry ground while the waters stand as walls. The pursuing army is drowned, and Israel sings of the LORD's victory.

antitype.name: Baptism into Christ
antitype.summary: Paul says Israel was 'baptised into Moses in the cloud and in the sea'. These things happened as examples (*typoi*) for us: believers are baptised into Christ and set free from sin's slavery.

correspondences.type: Passing through water out of slavery
correspondences.antitype: Passing through baptism out of sin's slavery

correspondences.type: The enemy drowned behind them
correspondences.antitype: Sin and the powers defeated

correspondences.type: Under the cloud of God's presence
correspondences.antitype: Baptised in the Spirit

correspondences.type: A song of victory on the far shore
correspondences.antitype: The song of Moses and of the Lamb (Rev 15:3)

differences: Paul's main point is a warning: all were baptised, yet most died in the wilderness. The type shows that the sign alone does not guarantee faithfulness. Israel's deliverance was national and physical; Christian baptism concerns each person's union with Christ.

fathers.note: Read the crossing as a figure of baptism, with Pharaoh's army as the devil left drowned in the water.
Preached the crossing as the soul passing through baptism and leaving the Egyptians, its vices, behind.
Taught newly baptised Christians that Pharaoh stands for the devil, and that in the font they had escaped him as Israel escaped Egypt.

plain: Israel walked through the sea and came out free on the other side, with the slave-masters gone for good. Paul says this was a kind of baptism. The point he presses is sober: they all got wet, but many did not keep trusting God afterwards, so do not presume.
caution: Paul uses the crossing to warn, not mainly to celebrate. The Fathers' detailed allegories (each Egyptian a particular vice) go well beyond Paul.

title: Manna and the bread of life

type.name: Manna in the wilderness
type.summary: God feeds Israel every morning with bread from heaven. It must be gathered daily, cannot be hoarded, and teaches that people do not live by bread alone but by every word from God's mouth.

antitype.name: Jesus, the bread of life
antitype.summary: After feeding five thousand, Jesus says the true bread from heaven is not Moses' manna but himself. Those who ate manna died; whoever eats this bread will live forever.

correspondences.type: Bread that comes down from heaven
correspondences.antitype: The Son who comes down from heaven

correspondences.type: Given daily, enough for each
correspondences.antitype: Sufficient for all who come

correspondences.type: Sustains life for a time
correspondences.antitype: Gives eternal life

correspondences.type: Kept in a jar in the ark as a memorial
correspondences.antitype: 'Hidden manna' promised to the faithful

differences: Jesus makes the contrast himself: the fathers ate manna and died. Manna fed bodies; Jesus speaks of himself as food for eternal life. Manna stopped when Israel entered the land; Christ's provision does not stop.

fathers.note: Preached that the manna and the Lord's bread are both signs, but that what matters is eating inwardly by faith, not merely outwardly.

source.author: Augustine
source.title: Tractates on the Gospel of John

fathers.note: Argued that the eucharist is greater than the manna, since manna was a shadow and the eucharist is the body of Christ.

plain: Manna was the daily bread God sent to keep Israel alive in the desert. Jesus says he is the real bread from heaven: not food that keeps you going one more day, but life that lasts forever.
caution: How far John 6 refers to the Lord's Supper is debated: Catholic and Orthodox readers see a strong eucharistic meaning; many Protestants read 'eating' mainly as believing (John 6:35). See /debates/lords-supper.

title: The rock that followed them

type.name: The rock that gave water
type.summary: At Rephidim Moses strikes a rock and water flows for the thirsty people. Later at Kadesh he is told to speak to the rock but strikes it twice, and is barred from the land.

antitype.name: Christ, the spiritual rock
antitype.summary: Paul says Israel drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, 'and the rock was Christ'. Jesus invites the thirsty to come and drink, and living water flows.

correspondences.type: Struck so that water flows
correspondences.antitype: Struck in death; from his side flow blood and water

correspondences.type: Water in a dry land for a complaining people
correspondences.antitype: Living water offered to the undeserving

correspondences.type: Follows the people through the wilderness
correspondences.antitype: Christ present with his people throughout their journey

differences: Paul's statement is unusual: he does not only say the rock pictured Christ but that Christ was present with Israel. The rock gave physical water; Christ gives the Spirit. Moses' second striking was an act of disobedience, so it cannot simply be read as 'Christ struck again'.

fathers.note: Commented that Paul did not say 'the rock signified Christ' but 'was Christ', and used this to explain how signs take the name of what they signify.

plain: In the desert, God gave Israel water from a rock. Paul says Christ was that rock: he was already there, providing for his people long before he was born in Bethlehem.
caution: Paul seems to draw on a Jewish tradition (found later in rabbinic writings) of a well or rock that travelled with Israel. Some popular preaching says 'the rock must be struck only once because Christ died once' from Numbers 20; this is a later application, not Paul's argument.

title: The bronze serpent lifted up

type.name: The bronze serpent on a pole
type.summary: When Israel is bitten by venomous snakes as judgement for their grumbling, God tells Moses to make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. Anyone bitten who looks at it lives.

antitype.name: The Son of Man lifted up on the cross
antitype.summary: Jesus says that as Moses lifted up the serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.

correspondences.type: Lifted up on a pole
correspondences.antitype: Lifted up on the cross

correspondences.type: Bitten people only need to look
correspondences.antitype: Sinners only need to believe

correspondences.type: The image of the deadly thing itself
correspondences.antitype: Christ 'made sin' for us (2 Cor 5:21)

correspondences.type: Remedy for death under judgement
correspondences.antitype: Remedy for perishing: eternal life

differences: The serpent was a lifeless object and later became an idol that Hezekiah destroyed. It healed physical bites for a time; Christ gives eternal life. The 'image of the curse' link is a reading of Paul, not stated by Jesus in John 3.

fathers.note: Argued the serpent was a sign of the cross, through which the power of the ancient serpent is broken.
Read the serpent as a figure of Jesus who would suffer and give life.
Saw the bronze serpent as Christ taking the likeness of sinful flesh to heal those wounded by sin.

plain: Dying people in the desert were told: look at the bronze snake on the pole and live. It sounds strange, but Jesus himself used the story to explain the cross. He would be lifted up, and anyone who looks to him in trust will live.
caution: The link is Jesus' own, but the fine detail of a serpent (a symbol of evil) standing for Christ puzzled ancient readers and has been explained in several ways. The serpent's later fate (2 Kgs 18:4) is a reminder that a sign can be turned into an idol.

title: The tabernacle: God dwelling among his people

type.name: The tabernacle (tent of meeting)
type.summary: God tells Moses to build a portable sanctuary exactly according to the pattern shown on the mountain, so that he may dwell among his people. When it is finished, the glory cloud fills it.

antitype.name: Christ's flesh and the heavenly sanctuary
antitype.summary: John says the Word became flesh and 'tabernacled' (pitched his tent) among us, and we saw his glory. Hebrews says the earthly tent was a copy and shadow of the true sanctuary in heaven, where Christ ministers.

correspondences.type: God pitches his tent among Israel
correspondences.antitype: The Word 'tents' among us in human flesh

correspondences.type: Glory fills the tent
correspondences.antitype: 'We have seen his glory'

correspondences.type: Built after a heavenly pattern
correspondences.antitype: Christ serves in the true, heavenly sanctuary

correspondences.type: God dwells with one nation in a tent
correspondences.antitype: God dwells with all peoples in the new creation

differences: The tabernacle restricted access: only priests, and only the high priest in the inner room. Christ opens access. The tent was temporary and made by hands; Hebrews says the true one is not of this creation.

fathers.note: Read every material of the tabernacle (gold, silver, bronze, fabrics) as a moral or spiritual lesson for the soul.
Wrote an entire commentary reading the tabernacle as a figure of the church in this present life.

plain: The tabernacle was a tent where God chose to live in the middle of Israel's camp. John uses the same idea for Jesus: in him God came to live among us. Hebrews adds that the tent was a scale model of something greater in heaven.
caution: The NT warrant is strong for the tabernacle as a whole. Detailed allegories of every board, socket and colour (common in older devotional books) go far beyond any NT text and should be treated as speculative.

title: The mercy seat and the place of atonement

type.name: The mercy seat (kapporet) on the ark
type.summary: The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, between the cherubim, where God promised to meet Moses. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled blood on it.

antitype.name: Christ set forth as hilasterion
antitype.summary: Paul says God put Christ forward as a *hilasterion* by his blood, to be received by faith. Hebrews uses the same Greek word for the mercy seat itself.

correspondences.type: Hidden inside the Most Holy Place
correspondences.antitype: Set forth publicly on the cross

correspondences.type: Blood sprinkled to cover sin
correspondences.antitype: 'By his blood' sin is dealt with

correspondences.type: Where God meets his people
correspondences.antitype: Christ is where God and humanity meet

correspondences.type: Covers the tablets of the law
correspondences.antitype: Sinners under the law find mercy in Christ

differences: The mercy seat was an object approached once a year by one man; Christ is offered openly to all through faith. The mercy seat was sprinkled with another's blood; Christ is both place and sacrifice.

fathers.note: Read Romans 3:25 as referring to the mercy seat and explained Christ as the true propitiatory, the place of God's meeting.

plain: Inside the holiest room of the tabernacle sat a gold lid on the ark, where blood was sprinkled once a year so that Israel's sins could be forgiven. Paul uses the same word for Jesus: the place where God deals with sin and shows mercy is now Jesus himself, out in the open.
caution: Scholars debate what *hilasterion* means in Romans 3:25: 'mercy seat' (the specific object, as in the Greek OT and Heb 9:5), 'propitiation' (a sacrifice that turns away wrath), or 'expiation' (a means of wiping away sin). This affects atonement theology; see /debates/atonement.

title: The Day of Atonement and the scapegoat

type.name: Yom Kippur
type.summary: Once a year the high priest offers a bull and a goat, carries their blood into the Most Holy Place, and sprinkles it on the mercy seat. He then lays both hands on a second goat, confesses Israel's sins over it, and sends it into the wilderness.

antitype.name: Christ's once-for-all offering
antitype.summary: Hebrews reads the day as a lesson: the yearly repetition proved the sacrifices could not perfect anyone. Christ entered heaven with his own blood once for all, and suffered outside the city gate like the sin offerings burned outside the camp.

correspondences.type: High priest enters once a year
correspondences.antitype: Christ enters once for all

correspondences.type: Blood of goats and bulls
correspondences.antitype: His own blood

correspondences.type: Bodies burned outside the camp
correspondences.antitype: Jesus suffers outside the gate

correspondences.type: Scapegoat carries sins away
correspondences.antitype: Christ bears sins and removes them (traditional reading)

correspondences.type: The people afflict themselves and rest
correspondences.antitype: Repentance and resting in a finished work

differences: Hebrews stresses that the old rite had to be repeated and could only cleanse outwardly. The scapegoat was not killed, while Christ was; this is why many readers see the two goats together as one picture: one for death, one for removal.

fathers.note: Read the two goats as Christ's two comings, and the scapegoat, spat on and crowned with scarlet wool in later Jewish practice, as Christ suffering.
Read the high priest's yearly entry as Christ's ascension into heaven with his own blood.

plain: On Israel's holiest day, blood was taken into God's presence and a goat carried the people's sins away into the desert. Hebrews says this was a yearly rehearsal for what Jesus did once: he took his own blood into the real presence of God and dealt with sin for good.
caution: Hebrews never mentions the scapegoat (Azazel goat); linking it to Christ is traditional, beginning with Barnabas. The meaning of 'Azazel' is debated (a place, 'complete removal', or a desert demon), and some early writers saw the scapegoat as a figure of something other than Christ.

title: The veil and the new way through

type.name: The curtain before the Most Holy Place
type.summary: A heavy embroidered curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place. No one could pass it except the high priest, once a year, with blood.

antitype.name: Christ's flesh, the opened way
antitype.summary: At Jesus' death the temple curtain is torn from top to bottom. Hebrews says believers now enter the holy places by his blood, through the new and living way he opened through the curtain, that is, his flesh.

correspondences.type: Barrier keeping people out
correspondences.antitype: Way opened for everyone who draws near

correspondences.type: Only the high priest may pass
correspondences.antitype: All believers may approach with confidence

correspondences.type: Curtain intact while the first tent stands
correspondences.antitype: Curtain torn when Christ dies

differences: The curtain hid God's presence; Christ's flesh reveals it. Hebrews' wording 'through the curtain, that is, his flesh' is compressed, and interpreters disagree whether his flesh is the curtain itself or the way through it.

fathers.note: Widely read the torn veil as the unveiling of the hidden meaning of the Scriptures and the opening of heaven.

plain: There was a curtain in the temple that said: keep out, God is holy. When Jesus died, it ripped from top to bottom. Hebrews says his death is the doorway: now anyone can come near to God through him.
caution: Whether the torn veil in the Gospels mainly means opened access, or judgement on the temple, or both, is debated. Matthew's text does not explain it; the meaning comes from Hebrews.

title: Firstfruits and the resurrection

type.name: The sheaf of firstfruits
type.summary: At the start of the barley harvest, the day after the Sabbath of Passover week, a priest waves the first sheaf before the LORD. It is the first part of the harvest, offered as a pledge that the rest belongs to God and will follow.

antitype.name: Christ raised as firstfruits
antitype.summary: Paul calls the risen Christ the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. His resurrection is the first sheaf of a harvest: those who belong to him will be raised at his coming.

correspondences.type: First sheaf of the harvest
correspondences.antitype: First person raised to the life of the age to come

correspondences.type: Offered the day after the Sabbath of Passover week
correspondences.antitype: Jesus rises on the first day of the week after Passover

correspondences.type: Guarantees the rest of the harvest
correspondences.antitype: Guarantees the resurrection of his people

differences: The sheaf was cut grain, already dead; Christ is the living risen one. The calendar link depends on how 'the day after the Sabbath' was reckoned, which Jewish groups disputed in Jesus' time.

fathers.note: Commonly connected the Easter season to the firstfruits and Pentecost cycle of fifty days, which shaped the Christian calendar from Easter to Pentecost.

plain: Farmers offered the first bundle of grain to God as a sign the whole harvest was coming. Paul says Jesus' resurrection is that first bundle: his rising is the promise that everyone who belongs to him will rise too.
caution: Paul uses the word 'firstfruits' but does not mention the festival day. The timing match (Jesus rising on the day of the sheaf offering) is attractive but depends on debated calendar questions.

title: Pentecost: the harvest feast and the gift of the Spirit

type.name: The Feast of Weeks (Shavuot)
type.summary: Fifty days after the firstfruits sheaf, Israel celebrates the wheat harvest with two loaves. In later Jewish tradition the feast also remembered the giving of the law at Sinai, roughly fifty days after the exodus.

antitype.name: The outpouring of the Spirit
antitype.summary: On the day of Pentecost the Spirit comes on the disciples with wind and fire, they speak in many languages, and three thousand people are added: the first great harvest of the church.

correspondences.type: Harvest festival
correspondences.antitype: Three thousand gathered in

correspondences.type: Sinai: fire, sound and God's voice
correspondences.antitype: Wind, tongues of fire and speech

correspondences.type: Law written on stone
correspondences.antitype: Spirit writing on hearts (2 Cor 3:3)

correspondences.type: At Sinai three thousand die after the golden calf
correspondences.antitype: At Pentecost three thousand receive life (a traditional observation)

differences: Luke does not explain why the Spirit came on Pentecost; he simply names the day. The Sinai link depends on a Jewish tradition that is only clearly attested after the NT period, though roots may be earlier (Jubilees ties covenant renewal to the feast).

fathers.note: Drew the parallel between the law given fifty days after Passover and the Spirit given fifty days after Easter, with the finger of God writing on stone and then on hearts.

source.author: Augustine
source.title: On the Spirit and the Letter

plain: Pentecost was already a Jewish holiday, a thanksgiving for the wheat harvest, before it became the Christian 'birthday of the church'. Luke tells us the Spirit came on that very day. Christians have seen a harvest of people and a new 'Sinai', with God's law now written on hearts.
caution: The Sinai–Pentecost parallel is widely held but is traditional and partly dependent on later Jewish sources; Acts itself does not spell it out. The 'three thousand' contrast with Exod 32:28 is a homiletic observation.

title: Tabernacles: water, light and God dwelling with us

type.name: The Feast of Booths (Sukkot)
type.summary: Israel lives in booths for a week to remember the wilderness and rejoices over the final harvest. By Jesus' day the feast included a daily water-pouring ceremony and great lamps lit in the temple courts. Zechariah pictures all nations keeping it.

antitype.name: Jesus, source of living water and light
antitype.summary: On the last great day of the feast, Jesus stands and cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink, speaking of the Spirit. Soon after he says, 'I am the light of the world'.

correspondences.type: Water poured out at the altar
correspondences.antitype: Rivers of living water: the Spirit

correspondences.type: Lamps lighting up Jerusalem
correspondences.antitype: 'I am the light of the world'

correspondences.type: Living in temporary booths
correspondences.antitype: The Word 'tented' among us

correspondences.type: Final harvest ingathering, all nations come
correspondences.antitype: A multitude from every nation, sheltered by God (Rev 7)

differences: The water and lamp rituals are known from the Mishnah (tractate Sukkah), not from the Old Testament; John assumes his readers know them. The feast looked back to the wilderness; John's Jesus points forward to the Spirit.

fathers.note: Treated the feast of booths as a figure of the resurrection and the final rest, when the righteous celebrate with God.

plain: Sukkot was a joyful week of camping out, harvest thanks, water-pouring and bright lights. At that very festival Jesus said: if you are thirsty, come to me; I am the light. John wants readers to see the festival's hopes coming true in Jesus.
caution: Some popular teaching claims Jesus was born at Tabernacles; this is speculation without solid evidence. The link to John 7-8 is strong but implicit; John never calls the festival a type.

title: The Sabbath and God's rest

type.name: The seventh-day Sabbath
type.summary: God rests on the seventh day of creation and makes it holy. Israel is commanded to stop work every seventh day, remembering both creation and freedom from slavery. Psalm 95 warns a disobedient generation that they will not enter God's rest.

antitype.name: The rest that remains for God's people
antitype.summary: Hebrews says a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God, entered by faith, in which they rest from their works as God did from his. Jesus offers rest to the weary and calls himself Lord of the Sabbath. Paul calls Sabbaths a shadow of things to come, the substance belonging to Christ.

correspondences.type: God's rest after finishing creation
correspondences.antitype: Believers rest in Christ's finished work

correspondences.type: Weekly stop from labour
correspondences.antitype: Rest offered to the weary and burdened

correspondences.type: Remembering release from slavery
correspondences.antitype: Release from sin's slavery

correspondences.type: The land's rest and Joshua's conquest
correspondences.antitype: A future rest that Joshua did not give

differences: The weekly Sabbath was physical and repeated; the rest in Hebrews is both present by faith and still future. Christians disagree on whether the weekly day itself is fulfilled and set aside, transferred to Sunday, or still binding on the seventh day.

fathers.note: Ended his *Confessions* and *City of God* with the eternal Sabbath, the seventh day without evening, as the goal of history.
Argued the true Sabbath is to cease from sin every day, rather than to keep one day idle.

plain: God built rest into the week. The NT says that weekly rest was a preview of a deeper rest: being at peace with God because of what Christ has done, and one day resting with God forever.
caution: How the typology applies to Christian practice is disputed: Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday; many Reformed and Presbyterian Christians see a 'Christian Sabbath' on Sunday; many others see Sabbath fulfilled in Christ without a binding day. The typology alone does not decide this.

title: Jubilee and the year of the Lord's favour

type.name: The Year of Jubilee
type.summary: Every fiftieth year, announced by a trumpet on the Day of Atonement, slaves are freed, debts are released and family land returns to its original owners. Isaiah 61 takes up this language for a coming anointed messenger who proclaims liberty.

antitype.name: Jesus' proclamation of release
antitype.summary: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah 61, 'to proclaim liberty to the captives... the acceptable year of the Lord', and says, 'Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing'.

correspondences.type: Liberty proclaimed throughout the land
correspondences.antitype: Freedom for captives and the oppressed

correspondences.type: Debts cancelled
correspondences.antitype: Forgiveness of sins (the same Greek word *aphesis*)

correspondences.type: Land returned to its families
correspondences.antitype: Restoration of all things

correspondences.type: Begins on the Day of Atonement
correspondences.antitype: Release grounded in atonement

differences: Jubilee was an economic law for land and slaves in Israel; there is little evidence it was regularly practised. Jesus quotes Isaiah rather than Leviticus. Interpreters disagree how far Jesus' 'release' is spiritual (forgiveness) and how far it carries social and economic demands.

fathers.note: Read the 'acceptable year' as the whole time of Christ's coming and preaching.

plain: Jubilee was meant to be Israel's great reset: slaves go home, debts are wiped, land returns to its families. Jesus began his public ministry by reading a passage built on this idea and saying it was happening now in him.
caution: Luke never uses the word 'jubilee'; the link runs through Isaiah 61, which itself echoes Leviticus 25. Some modern movements read Luke 4 mainly as a social programme, others mainly as forgiveness of sins. Both have textual footholds.

title: Joshua and Jesus: the same name

type.name: Joshua son of Nun
type.summary: Moses renames Hoshea 'Joshua' (the LORD saves). After Moses dies, Joshua leads Israel across the Jordan into the promised land and gives them rest from their enemies.

antitype.name: Jesus, who brings the true rest
antitype.summary: Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua. Hebrews points out that if Joshua had given Israel the final rest, God would not have spoken of another day; that rest comes through Jesus.

correspondences.type: Name means 'the LORD saves'
correspondences.antitype: 'He will save his people from their sins'

correspondences.type: Succeeds Moses, who could not bring them in
correspondences.antitype: Brings what the law could not

correspondences.type: Crosses the Jordan to begin the conquest
correspondences.antitype: Baptised in the Jordan to begin his ministry

correspondences.type: Leads the people into the inheritance
correspondences.antitype: Leads his people into God's rest

differences: Hebrews uses Joshua mainly by contrast: his rest was incomplete. Joshua's conquest was by the sword against Canaanite cities; Jesus wins by dying and forbids his followers to fight with the sword.

fathers.note: Stressed that Moses gave the name Jesus (Joshua) to Hoshea as a prophetic sign of the one to come.
Preached a whole series on Joshua as a figure of Jesus leading the soul into its inheritance after the law (Moses) has died.

plain: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name. Joshua took Israel into the land Moses could only see. Hebrews says even that was not the final rest; Jesus brings the rest that Joshua could not.
caution: Older English Bibles (KJV) translate Heb 4:8 and Acts 7:45 as 'Jesus', which confuses readers; the meaning there is Joshua. Reading the conquest's violence as a model for Christians is a misuse of the typology.

title: Boaz the kinsman-redeemer

type.name: Boaz, the go'el
type.summary: Boaz, a relative of Naomi's dead husband, acts as 'redeemer' (go'el): he buys back the family land, marries Ruth the Moabite widow, and so restores the family line, from which David comes.

antitype.name: Christ the redeemer
antitype.summary: Christ becomes our kin by sharing flesh and blood, pays the price to redeem, and takes a bride drawn from all nations. Boaz appears in Jesus' genealogy.

correspondences.type: Must be a close relative
correspondences.antitype: The Son shares our flesh and blood

correspondences.type: Willing and able to pay
correspondences.antitype: Pays with his own life

correspondences.type: Spreads his 'wing' (garment) over Ruth
correspondences.antitype: Shelter under God's wings (Ruth 2:12)

correspondences.type: Takes a foreign woman into Israel
correspondences.antitype: Gentiles brought into God's people

correspondences.type: A nearer kinsman cannot redeem
correspondences.antitype: The law could not save (Rom 8:3)

differences: Boaz's redemption was a legal, economic and family transaction with no sin or atonement in view. Ruth was not rescued from guilt but from poverty. The NT never cites Ruth for redemption.

fathers.note: Saw Ruth the foreigner as a figure of the gentile church joined to Christ.

source.author: Ambrose
source.title: Exposition of the Gospel of Luke

fathers.note: The Targum and Ruth Rabbah connect Ruth's line with the coming Messiah through David, a messianic reading from within Judaism.

plain: In Israel, if you lost your land or your family name was dying out, a close relative could step in and 'redeem' you. Boaz did that for Ruth and Naomi. Christians see Jesus doing the same: becoming our relative, paying the price and bringing outsiders into the family.
caution: Traditional with no direct NT warrant. The word 'redeem' in the NT draws more on the exodus and slave-release than on Ruth. Some popular readings sexualise or over-allegorise the threshing-floor scene; the text itself is reserved.

title: David, the shepherd-king

type.name: David
type.summary: The youngest son, a shepherd boy, anointed king, who defeats Goliath, suffers persecution, and receives God's promise that his throne will last forever. The prophets later speak of a coming 'David' who will shepherd God's people.

antitype.name: Jesus, son of David and good shepherd
antitype.summary: Jesus is hailed as son of David, born in David's town, and claims to be the good shepherd who lays down his life. Peter argues that David, being a prophet, spoke of the Messiah's resurrection.

correspondences.type: Shepherd of his father's flock
correspondences.antitype: The good shepherd

correspondences.type: Anointed but not yet enthroned, hunted by Saul
correspondences.antitype: Anointed Messiah, rejected before exaltation

correspondences.type: Defeats the giant on Israel's behalf
correspondences.antitype: Defeats the enemy his people could not face

correspondences.type: Promised an everlasting throne
correspondences.antitype: Reigns forever

correspondences.type: Psalms of suffering (Ps 22)
correspondences.antitype: Jesus prays Psalm 22 on the cross

differences: David committed adultery and murder, and his family was torn by violence. Jesus himself said the Messiah is David's Lord, not merely his son. David's kingdom was national and fought with the sword.

fathers.note: Includes David hunted as one of the figures in whom Christ suffered beforehand.
Read the Psalms as the voice of the whole Christ, head and body, often heard first in David's mouth.

plain: David went from shepherd boy to king and was promised a dynasty that would never end. Israel's hopes for a Messiah grew from that promise. The NT presents Jesus as the son of David who finally fulfils it: a shepherd-king who gives his life for his sheep.
caution: The David–Messiah link is clear in the NT, but reading every detail of David's life (e.g. the five stones, or particular battles) as Christological is a later devotional move. The Goliath parallel is traditional, not stated in the NT.

title: Solomon, son of David and temple-builder

type.name: Solomon
type.summary: David's son, promised that he would build a house for God's name and that God would be his father. He is famed for wisdom, peace and wealth, builds the temple, and the queen of Sheba comes from far away to hear him. Later he falls into idolatry.

antitype.name: Jesus, greater than Solomon
antitype.summary: Jesus says 'something greater than Solomon is here'. Hebrews applies God's promise to Solomon, 'I will be his father, and he shall be my son', to Christ. Jesus speaks of raising a temple, his body, and builds his church as God's house.

correspondences.type: Son of David
correspondences.antitype: Son of David

correspondences.type: Builds a house for God
correspondences.antitype: Builds his church, a living temple

correspondences.type: Famed for wisdom
correspondences.antitype: In him are all treasures of wisdom

correspondences.type: Kingdom of peace (shalom)
correspondences.antitype: Prince of peace

correspondences.type: Gentile queen comes to hear his wisdom
correspondences.antitype: Nations come to hear Christ

differences: Solomon's heart turned to other gods and his kingdom split after his death. 2 Sam 7:14 even mentions punishment for the son's iniquity, which Hebrews does not quote and cannot apply to Christ. Solomon used forced labour to build.

fathers.note: Argued that the promise to David was only partly fulfilled in Solomon and pointed beyond him to Christ, since Solomon's reign did not last forever.

plain: Solomon was David's son, built God's temple and was the wisest king Israel ever had. But he failed badly in the end. Jesus pointed to Solomon and said, in effect: I am the greater son of David, the true wisdom, and the one who builds God's real house.
caution: Allegorical readings of the Song of Songs (Solomon as Christ, the bride as the church or soul) are a separate and debated tradition, not part of the NT typology.

title: The sign of Jonah

type.name: Jonah in the fish
type.summary: Jonah is thrown into the sea to save the sailors, swallowed by a great fish, and after three days and three nights is spat out alive. He then preaches to Nineveh, which repents.

antitype.name: Jesus' death, burial and resurrection
antitype.summary: Asked for a sign, Jesus says no sign will be given but the sign of Jonah: as Jonah was three days and nights in the fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and nights in the heart of the earth. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and something greater than Jonah is here.

correspondences.type: Thrown overboard so the others are saved
correspondences.antitype: Dies so that others are saved

correspondences.type: Three days in the depths
correspondences.antitype: Three days in the grave

correspondences.type: Comes back from the deep
correspondences.antitype: Rises from the dead

correspondences.type: Gentile city repents
correspondences.antitype: Gospel goes to the nations

differences: Jonah was running from God and resented Nineveh's mercy; Jesus went willingly and wept over his city. Jonah was cast out for his own sin; Jesus was without sin.

fathers.note: In his commentary on Jonah, read the prophet as a figure of Christ's passion and resurrection, while noting where Jonah's flight cannot fit Christ.

plain: Jonah spent three days inside a great fish and came out alive. Jesus said his own death and resurrection would be 'the sign of Jonah'. It is one of the few types Jesus names himself.
caution: 'Three days and three nights' is a Jewish way of counting parts of days; it does not require 72 hours, so it does not force a Wednesday crucifixion. Luke's version stresses Jonah's preaching as the sign rather than the fish.

title: Elijah and John the Baptist

type.name: Elijah the prophet
type.summary: A rugged prophet in a hairy garment with a leather belt, who confronts King Ahab and Jezebel, calls Israel back from Baal, and is taken to heaven in a whirlwind. Malachi promises God will send Elijah before the great day of the LORD.

antitype.name: John the Baptist, forerunner of the Messiah
antitype.summary: John appears in the wilderness dressed like Elijah, calls the nation to repent, and confronts King Herod and Herodias. Jesus says that if they are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come.

correspondences.type: Camel-hair garment and leather belt
correspondences.antitype: Camel-hair garment and leather belt

correspondences.type: Calls Israel back to God
correspondences.antitype: Turns hearts of fathers to children

correspondences.type: Opposed by a king and his scheming queen
correspondences.antitype: Imprisoned and killed through Herod and Herodias

correspondences.type: Hands over to a successor at the Jordan
correspondences.antitype: Baptises Jesus at the Jordan and steps back

differences: John himself denied being Elijah when asked (John 1:21), probably meaning he was not Elijah returned in person. Luke clarifies: he came 'in the spirit and power of Elijah'. Elijah did not die; John was executed.

fathers.note: Explained John's denial and Jesus' affirmation by saying John had Elijah's spirit and power, not Elijah's soul, and rejected reincarnation.

plain: The last OT prophet promised that Elijah would come back before the Lord arrived. John the Baptist dressed like Elijah, preached like Elijah and stood up to a king like Elijah. Jesus said: he is the Elijah you were waiting for.
caution: This does not support reincarnation; Luke 1:17 speaks of 'the spirit and power of Elijah'. Some traditions also expect Elijah to return personally before the end (Rev 11 is sometimes read this way); that is a separate, debated question.

title: Cities of refuge

type.name: The six cities of refuge
type.summary: Six towns were set apart where someone who killed another person by accident could flee from the avenger of blood. Inside, they were safe; they could go home freely after the death of the high priest.

antitype.name: Refuge in Christ
antitype.summary: Hebrews speaks of believers as those who 'have fled for refuge' to lay hold of the hope set before them, an anchor that reaches behind the curtain where Jesus has entered as high priest.

correspondences.type: Open to Israelite and foreigner alike
correspondences.antitype: Open to all who come

correspondences.type: Safe only inside the city
correspondences.antitype: No condemnation for those in Christ

correspondences.type: Freedom comes through the death of the high priest
correspondences.antitype: Freedom through the death of our high priest

correspondences.type: Roads kept clear and signposted (later Jewish tradition)
correspondences.antitype: The way to Christ made plain

differences: The cities protected the unintentional killer only; a deliberate murderer was handed over. The gospel offers refuge to the guilty, not only to the accidental offender. Hebrews' 'fled for refuge' may be an echo, but it does not name the cities.

fathers.note: Read the high priest's death that frees the refugee as a figure of Christ's death that frees sinners.

plain: Israel had safe towns where someone who had killed a person by accident could run and be protected. Christians have seen in them a picture of running to Christ for safety. The death of the high priest set the refugee free, which many find a striking echo of Jesus.
caution: Traditional, not explicit. The detail about clear roads and signposts comes from the Mishnah (tractate Makkot), not the OT. The fit is imperfect, since the refuge was for the innocent-but-liable, not for the wicked.

title: The temple, Christ's body and the church

type.name: The Jerusalem temple
type.summary: The temple in Jerusalem is the place where God puts his name and his glory dwells, where sacrifice is offered and prayer is heard. The prophets see its glory leave before the exile and promise a greater glory in a future house.

antitype.name: Jesus' body, the church, and the new Jerusalem
antitype.summary: Jesus speaks of destroying 'this temple' and raising it in three days, meaning his body. Paul calls the church and the believer's body God's temple, built on Christ the cornerstone. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, for God and the Lamb are its temple.

correspondences.type: Where God's glory dwells
correspondences.antitype: God's fullness dwells bodily in Christ

correspondences.type: Built of costly stones
correspondences.antitype: Believers as living stones

correspondences.type: Where sacrifice is offered
correspondences.antitype: Spiritual sacrifices offered through Christ

correspondences.type: Destroyed and rebuilt
correspondences.antitype: Body destroyed and raised in three days

correspondences.type: God's presence limited to one place
correspondences.antitype: Whole new creation filled with God's presence

differences: The temple could be defiled, destroyed and abandoned by the glory; the NT presents the risen Christ as a temple that cannot be destroyed again. The temple was made with hands; the new one is 'not made with hands' (Mark 14:58).

fathers.note: Read John 2 as a picture of the whole body of Christ, the church, destroyed and raised.
Read the building of the temple as the building up of the church out of living stones from all nations.

plain: The temple was the place where heaven and earth met. The NT says that meeting place is now Jesus himself, and through him his people, and in the end the whole renewed world, where God lives with his people without any wall.
caution: Christians disagree about whether a future rebuilt temple in Jerusalem has a role in prophecy; dispensationalists often say yes, many others say the typology means the physical temple's role is fulfilled. See /debates/israel-and-church and /debates/millennium.

title: Jacob's ladder and the Son of Man

type.name: Jacob's ladder at Bethel
type.summary: Fleeing from Esau, Jacob dreams of a stairway set on the earth reaching to heaven, with God's angels going up and down on it. He wakes and says this is the house of God and the gate of heaven.

antitype.name: Jesus, the link between heaven and earth
antitype.summary: Jesus tells Nathanael, an 'Israelite in whom is no deceit', that he will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

correspondences.type: A stairway joining earth and heaven
correspondences.antitype: The Son of Man joins earth and heaven

correspondences.type: Angels going up and down on it
correspondences.antitype: Angels going up and down on the Son of Man

correspondences.type: Bethel, 'house of God'
correspondences.antitype: Jesus, where God dwells (John 1:14)

correspondences.type: Given to Jacob the deceiver
correspondences.antitype: Promised to Nathanael, an Israelite without deceit

differences: Jacob's ladder was a dream vision; Jesus is a person. The ladder simply stood there; Jesus is mediator by his own life and death.

fathers.note: Read the angels ascending and descending on the Son of Man as preachers lifting up Christ the head in heaven and coming down to Christ's body on earth.

source.author: Augustine
source.title: Tractates on the Gospel of John

plain: Jacob dreamed of a stairway between heaven and earth. Jesus told his first disciples: you will see that I am that stairway. He is the way God comes down to us and we come up to God.
caution: Later devotional readings that turn each rung into a stage of spiritual progress (as in some monastic writings) are a separate tradition and not part of John's meaning.

title: The sacrificial system and the one sacrifice

type.name: Israel's offerings
type.summary: Leviticus sets out burnt, grain, peace, sin and guilt offerings. Blood is given 'to make atonement for your souls'. Yet the prophets and psalms also say God does not ultimately desire animal sacrifice but an obedient heart.

antitype.name: Christ's once-for-all offering
antitype.summary: Hebrews says the law has only a shadow of the good things to come. Animal blood cannot take away sins; Christ, coming to do God's will, offered his own body once for all and sat down.

correspondences.type: Unblemished animals
correspondences.antitype: A sinless offering

correspondences.type: The worshipper lays hands on the victim
correspondences.antitype: Identification of sinners with Christ

correspondences.type: Repeated daily and yearly
correspondences.antitype: Offered once for all

correspondences.type: Priests always standing
correspondences.antitype: Christ sat down: the work is finished

correspondences.type: Peace offering shared in a meal
correspondences.antitype: Fellowship with God through Christ

differences: Hebrews says the old sacrifices could never perfect the conscience; they served as a reminder of sin. Christ's offering was a person freely doing God's will, which Psalm 40 already hinted was what God truly wanted.

fathers.note: Summed up the relation of the Testaments in a famous saying, often paraphrased: the New lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. He applied this to the sacrifices as signs of the one true sacrifice.
Defined a visible sacrifice as the sacrament, or sacred sign, of an invisible sacrifice, and said all the old sacrifices signified the one sacrifice of Christ.

plain: Israel's worship was full of sacrifices. Hebrews says they were like shadows cast ahead of a person who was coming. The shadow had the right shape, but it was not the real thing. When Christ came and gave himself, the shadow had done its job.
caution: Christians agree Christ's sacrifice fulfils the system, but differ on how the eucharist relates to it (a re-presentation of the one sacrifice in Catholic and Orthodox teaching; a memorial or spiritual feeding in most Protestant teaching). Not every detail of each offering needs a Christological meaning.

title: Circumcision, the circumcised heart and baptism

type.name: Circumcision
type.summary: Circumcision is the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's household, given to boys on the eighth day. Already in the OT, Moses and the prophets call for a circumcised heart, and Deuteronomy promises God will circumcise his people's hearts.

antitype.name: Circumcision of the heart by Christ
antitype.summary: Paul says believers have been circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by the putting off of the body of the flesh, the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism. True circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit.

correspondences.type: A cutting away in the flesh
correspondences.antitype: Putting off the old self

correspondences.type: Sign of entry into the covenant people
correspondences.antitype: Baptism marks entry into Christ

correspondences.type: Done by human hands
correspondences.antitype: Done 'without hands' by Christ and the Spirit

correspondences.type: On the eighth day
correspondences.antitype: New creation on the 'eighth day' of resurrection (traditional)

differences: Circumcision was given to males of Abraham's household; baptism is given to men and women alike (Gal 3:27-28). Paul insists outward circumcision without the heart is worthless, so the true antitype is inward change, with baptism as its sign.

fathers.note: Argued Christians have received a spiritual circumcision through baptism, which Enoch and others had without fleshly circumcision.
Used the eighth-day timing of circumcision in debate about whether infants could be baptised before the eighth day; his council said they could.

plain: Circumcision marked a boy as part of God's covenant people. Even in the OT, God said what he really wanted was a 'circumcised heart'. Paul says Christ does that inner surgery, and baptism is now the outward sign of belonging.
caution: Whether Colossians 2 makes baptism the direct replacement of circumcision is central to the infant-baptism debate: paedobaptists see continuity of the covenant sign to children; credobaptists argue the antitype is the inward circumcision of believers only. See /debates/baptism.

title: The exodus and salvation in Christ

type.name: The exodus from Egypt
type.summary: God hears Israel's cry, judges Egypt, rescues his people through the Passover and the sea, and brings them to Sinai to be his treasured possession. The prophets later promise a new and greater exodus from exile.

antitype.name: Redemption through Christ
antitype.summary: At the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah speak with Jesus about his 'departure' (Greek *exodos*) to be accomplished at Jerusalem. Believers are rescued from the domain of darkness and made a royal priesthood, the very titles given to Israel at Sinai.

correspondences.type: Slavery in Egypt
correspondences.antitype: Slavery to sin and death

correspondences.type: Passover blood
correspondences.antitype: Christ's blood

correspondences.type: Through the sea
correspondences.antitype: Through baptism

correspondences.type: Wilderness testing
correspondences.antitype: The Christian life as pilgrimage

correspondences.type: Made a kingdom of priests at Sinai
correspondences.antitype: Made a royal priesthood

differences: The exodus freed a single nation from a political oppressor; the NT speaks of freedom from sin and death for people of every nation. Israel's wilderness generation largely fell away, which Paul uses as a warning rather than a promise.

fathers.note: Retold the whole exodus night as the outline of the gospel, with Egypt's firstborn struck and Israel kept by the lamb's blood.
Read the exodus as the soul's journey out of slavery to the passions toward God.

plain: The exodus is the great rescue story of the OT. The NT tells the story of Jesus with the same shape: a lamb, a crossing through water, a journey, a people made God's own. Luke even calls Jesus' death and resurrection his 'exodus'.
caution: Liberation theologies read the exodus primarily as God's rescue of the poor and oppressed in history, while other traditions stress its spiritual fulfilment. The NT supports a spiritual reading clearly; how far the political dimension carries over is debated.

title: The promised land and the inheritance to come

type.name: Canaan, the promised land
type.summary: God promises Abraham's descendants the land of Canaan, a good land flowing with milk and honey. Under Joshua Israel enters it and receives rest, though the hold on it is always conditional and is later lost in exile.

antitype.name: The inheritance and the new creation
antitype.summary: Paul says Abraham was promised he would inherit 'the world'. Jesus says the meek will inherit the earth. Hebrews says the patriarchs were looking for a better, heavenly country, a city God has prepared. Revelation ends with a new heaven and new earth.

correspondences.type: A land promised to Abraham's offspring
correspondences.antitype: The world promised to all who share Abraham's faith

correspondences.type: Rest from enemies
correspondences.antitype: The rest that remains

correspondences.type: Inheritance divided by lot
correspondences.antitype: An inheritance kept in heaven, imperishable

correspondences.type: God dwelling in the land among his people
correspondences.antitype: God dwelling with humanity in the new creation

differences: Canaan could be lost through disobedience and was entered by conquest. The NT inheritance is 'imperishable, undefiled and unfading' and global in scope.

fathers.note: Insisted the promise of land to Abraham will be fulfilled literally in a renewed earth at the resurrection, against those who spiritualised it away.
Read the land mainly as the soul's spiritual inheritance and heavenly realities, a reading Irenaeus' approach resisted.

plain: God promised Abraham a land. The NT says the promise was bigger than a strip of the Middle East: it pointed to the whole renewed earth, which all of Abraham's spiritual children will inherit.
caution: Whether the typology means the land promise to ethnic Israel is fulfilled and widened, or still awaits a specific future fulfilment, is a live debate between covenant theology, dispensationalism and others, with real political consequences today. See /debates/israel-and-church.

title: Hagar and Sarah: Paul's allegory of two covenants

type.name: Hagar and Sarah, Ishmael and Isaac
type.summary: Abraham has a son by Hagar the Egyptian slave woman, born in the ordinary way, and later a son by Sarah the free woman, born by God's promise in old age. Hagar and Ishmael are eventually sent away.

antitype.name: Two covenants: slavery and freedom
antitype.summary: Paul says these things may be read allegorically: the two women are two covenants. Hagar stands for Mount Sinai and the present Jerusalem, in slavery; Sarah for the Jerusalem above, which is free and is our mother. Believers are children of promise like Isaac.

correspondences.type: Hagar the slave
correspondences.antitype: The covenant from Sinai, bearing children for slavery

correspondences.type: Sarah the free woman
correspondences.antitype: The Jerusalem above, mother of the free

correspondences.type: Ishmael born 'according to the flesh'
correspondences.antitype: Trying to belong to God by human effort

correspondences.type: Isaac born by promise
correspondences.antitype: Believers born by the Spirit

correspondences.type: Ishmael mocks Isaac
correspondences.antitype: Those of the flesh persecute those of the Spirit

differences: Paul's reading reverses what his opponents would have expected: they would identify Jews with Sarah's line. In Genesis, God also cares for Hagar and Ishmael, sees Hagar's misery and blesses Ishmael (Gen 16:13; Gen 21:17-20), which Paul's argument does not address.

fathers.note: Cited Galatians 4 as proof that the apostles themselves read the OT allegorically, giving licence for his wider method.
Noted that Paul used the word 'allegory' loosely, meaning a type, and that the history still really happened.

plain: Paul takes the story of Abraham's two wives and two sons and uses it as a picture. One son was born from human planning, the other from God's promise. Paul says trying to be right with God through the law is like being Hagar's child; trusting God's promise makes you Sarah's child, free.
caution: This is Paul's own allegory (he uses the word *allēgoroumena*) in a heated argument against teachers urging gentiles to be circumcised.
