It has been misused to cast the Jewish people as 'slaves' or rejected; Paul's target is a specific teaching, and Romans 9-11 shows his ongoing hope for Israel. It is also not a licence to allegorise any story at will.

title: Israel, God's son, and Jesus the true Israel

type.name: Israel as God's firstborn son
type.summary: God calls Israel 'my firstborn son' and brings him out of Egypt. In the wilderness Israel is tested for forty years and often fails. Isaiah speaks of the servant who is called 'Israel'.

antitype.name: Jesus, the faithful Son
antitype.summary: Matthew says Jesus' return from Egypt fulfils 'Out of Egypt I called my son'. After passing through the waters of baptism, Jesus is tested forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation with Deuteronomy, succeeding where Israel failed.

correspondences.type: God's son called out of Egypt
correspondences.antitype: Jesus brought back from Egypt

correspondences.type: Passes through the sea
correspondences.antitype: Passes through the Jordan in baptism

correspondences.type: Forty years tested in the wilderness
correspondences.antitype: Forty days tested in the wilderness

correspondences.type: Grumbles for bread, tests God, worships the calf
correspondences.antitype: Refuses each temptation, quoting Deut 8:3, 6:16, 6:13

correspondences.type: Israel as God's vine
correspondences.antitype: 'I am the true vine'

differences: Hosea 11:1 in context looks back on Israel's past; it is not a prediction. Matthew reads it as a pattern Jesus relives and completes. Israel was a disobedient son; Jesus is the obedient one.

fathers.note: Discussed whether Matthew drew Hosea 11:1 from the Hebrew rather than the Greek OT (which reads 'his children'), and defended Matthew's use.

plain: Hosea was remembering the exodus when he wrote 'out of Egypt I called my son'. Matthew sees Jesus walking the same road Israel walked: out of Egypt, through the water, into the wilderness. But where Israel stumbled, Jesus stays faithful. He sums up Israel in himself.
caution: Matthew's 'fulfilled' here does not mean Hosea made a prediction; it means the pattern reaches its full meaning in Jesus. Seeing Jesus as 'true Israel' is sometimes pushed into replacement theology (the church replaces Israel); many interpreters who accept this typology reject that conclusion. See /debates/israel-and-church.

title: Rahab's scarlet cord

type.name: The scarlet cord in Rahab's window
type.summary: Rahab, a Canaanite woman of Jericho, hides Israel's spies. They tell her to tie a scarlet cord in her window; everyone in her house when the city falls will be spared.

antitype.name: Redemption through Christ's blood
antitype.summary: The NT honours Rahab for her faith and her actions and places her in Jesus' family line. Early Christians read the scarlet cord as a sign of redemption through the blood of the Lord.

correspondences.type: A red sign on the house keeps those inside safe
correspondences.antitype: Christ's blood protects those who shelter in him

correspondences.type: Like the Passover blood on the doorposts
correspondences.antitype: Echo of Christ our Passover

correspondences.type: A gentile outsider is brought into Israel
correspondences.antitype: Gentiles brought into God's people

differences: The NT praises Rahab's faith and hospitality but never mentions the cord. The cord was a practical signal for soldiers, not a sacrifice.

fathers.note: Said the scarlet thread made plain that redemption would come through the blood of the Lord to all who believe and hope in God, and that Rahab showed both faith and prophecy.
Made the same link between the scarlet sign and the blood of Christ.
Read Rahab's house as the church, outside of which no one is saved.

plain: Rahab hung a red cord in her window and her family survived when Jericho fell. Christians very early on saw a picture of being kept safe by Christ's blood. It is a lovely image, but it comes from the early church, not from the NT.
caution: A good example of a traditional type: 1 Clement 12 (around AD 96) makes the link, but no NT writer does. It is fine as illustration, but it should not be taught as if the Bible itself said it. Origen's 'no salvation outside Rahab's house' is a further application.
